rows.why: The internal decisions and workflows (HR, finance, approvals, operations) that AI output feeds are documented with their purpose and business value, the task the AI performs in them (such as scoring, classifying, summarising or recommending), the staff who use it and the people those decisions affect.
The business value of using AI output in each internal workflow, and what decisions and data depend on it, are defined.

Requirements for how staff work with AI output in each internal process (review steps, override, which decisions a person must make) are gathered from the staff who use it and the people its decisions affect before the process relies on it.
Staff using AI output in internal processes are told its knowledge limits and how they should check, challenge and override it before acting on it.
The expected benefit of using AI output in each internal process is examined against the staff-only baseline, so its use is justified by the process and not by habit.

The likelihood and size of both the costs and the benefits of AI output in internal decisions (HR, finance, approvals, operations) are examined, using past use and feedback, so high-impact decisions are identified.
The internal decisions AI output may and may not be used for are specified, so staff do not stretch it to decisions it was not meant to drive.
Human review of AI output in internal workflows is defined, including which decisions need a named person to check and sign off before they take effect.
Internal decisions made on AI output are rated by likelihood and magnitude of harm to staff and others affected, so high-impact decisions are known and treated differently.
High-impact internal decisions made on AI output are regularly assessed by people independent of the process owners, such as internal audit or an independent reviewer.
The human-AI workflow, with staff checking and overriding AI output, is tried out with real staff under real working conditions (volume, time pressure) before go-live, and the results are documented.
Decisions made on AI output are recorded with who reviewed, accepted or overrode it, and the records are reviewed so high-impact decisions and insider misuse can be audited.
Staff receive AI output with enough context (reasons, sources, confidence) to interpret it in their process and challenge it rather than accept it as is.
Staff and the people affected by internal decisions made on AI output can report problems and appeal those decisions, and the reports are counted and analysed.

Over-reliance is measured: how often staff override or accept AI output unchanged in internal processes, and what they report about trusting it, and the results are used, with the staff involved, to change the process, its review steps or the AI use.
Each internal process using AI output is periodically judged on whether it meets its purpose and whether the AI use should continue, change or stop.
Business rules in the workflow limit what AI output can decide on its own, such as thresholds above which a human approval is enforced before the decision takes effect.
Staff can set aside AI output and the process can fall back to a manual route when the output proves unreliable, with named people deciding when to do so.
Each internal process using AI output has a monitoring plan after go-live covering staff feedback, appeals and overrides, changes to the process or AI use, incident handling and retiring the AI use.
Wrong decisions made on AI output are tracked as incidents, communicated to the people affected, corrected and reviewed afterwards.
The known limits of the coding assistant (invented packages and APIs, outdated or unsafe patterns) are documented for developers so they know what to check before using its output.
The benefits expected from AI code generation (developer productivity, code quality) are examined and documented, so they can be weighed against what it actually delivers.
Which repositories, languages and coding tasks AI code generation may be used for, and where it is not allowed, are specified and documented.
The human oversight of AI-generated code is defined: who must review and approve it before merge, and how AI-written code and artifacts are marked so the review is not skipped.
Dependencies the AI suggests are checked for existence, provenance and trust before use, and licence or intellectual property risks of generated code are identified and documented.
Dependencies suggested by the AI are checked against approved sources and for known vulnerabilities before they are used.
The use of AI code generation is monitored in practice, for example suggested dependencies that do not exist, secrets reaching prompts, and AI-generated changes later reverted or tied to defects.
AI-assisted changes are traceable: assistant activity and any code it executes are logged, and commits record that AI was used and who reviewed and merged them.
Developers have a way to report unsafe or invented suggestions and leaked secrets from the coding assistant, and these reports feed into how its use is evaluated.
From what has been mapped and monitored, the organisation decides whether the coding assistant meets its purpose and whether its use should continue, be restricted or stop.
The organisation can disable the coding assistant or withdraw its access to repositories and credentials when it produces unsafe output, with assigned responsibility and defined thresholds.
Incidents from AI-generated code, such as a malicious package it suggested or a secret sent in a prompt, are tracked, responded to (removal, secret rotation) and reviewed afterwards.
Each customer-facing AI use is documented with its purpose, the public users it serves and their expectations, and the consumer laws and norms that apply to answers given directly to customers.
The business value of the customer-facing AI, and how its answers are used further by customers and the business, are defined.
Requirements for the customer-facing AI (telling customers they talk to AI, never disclosing other customers' data, handing off to a person) are set before it is built or deployed.
The knowledge limits of the customer-facing AI and the questions it must not answer are documented and made clear to customers, so they know when not to act on an answer.
The benefits customers are meant to get from the AI are examined, with customer input on what they value, so they can be weighed against the harms.
The topics, channels and customer groups the public AI may serve are deliberately narrowed, taking into account the likelihood of misuse and abuse by public users.
The customer-facing answers and actions that are high-impact and need human review or hand-off before they reach or affect the customer are identified and documented.
The likelihood and magnitude of harm from public attacks (prompt injection, abuse) and from wrong, harmful or leaked answers reaching customers are assessed and documented.
Performance of the customer-facing AI is measured under real public conditions (unexpected, non-optimised use by customers), not only in the lab.
Live customer conversations are monitored for abuse patterns, brute-force or extraction prompting and unreliable answers, with alerts when behaviour departs from what was tested.
The customer-facing AI is tested to fail safely when asked beyond its limits or provoked, refusing or handing off rather than giving harmful answers to customers.
The public-facing AI is red-teamed and penetration-tested for prompt injection, jailbreaks, abuse and data leakage by outside users, and the results are documented.
Customer conversations and high-impact answers are logged with enough detail, and human reviews and overrides recorded, so what a customer was told can be audited and traced.
Leaks of personal or confidential data in answers to customers are monitored and examined.
Customers have a way to report wrong or harmful answers and appeal outcomes, and these reports are counted, categorised and used in evaluating the customer-facing AI.
Customer feedback, positive and negative, and how often answers are overridden are used to check that the application performs as intended in front of customers.
Guardrails, business rules and throttling restrict what the customer-facing AI can say or do and separate untrusted public input from system instructions.
The customer-facing AI can be quickly switched off or bypassed to a human channel when it misbehaves, with set thresholds and named people who decide.
Post-deployment monitoring of the customer-facing AI is run in practice, capturing customer input, appeal and override, and changes to the application.
Customer complaints and negative feedback lead to measurable changes in the customer-facing AI's guardrails, scope and hand-off rules in its updates.
Incidents where customers received wrong, harmful or leaked answers are tracked, responded to, reviewed and communicated to the affected customers.
For each vendor product, the AI features in use are documented: what each is for, who uses it, and which of the org's data and processes it acts on.
The business purpose each vendor AI feature serves in internal processes is decided and owned.
The org sets requirements for vendor AI (no training on its data, retention limits, data residency, notice of AI changes) and puts them to the vendor before the feature is used.
Which org data each vendor AI feature reads and where it goes, including the vendor's own model provider, is documented as a data flow and dependency.
Each vendor AI feature is scoped to the systems, data classes and uses it may touch, so the data it is exposed to is limited.
The vendor AI features that act on the org's data (changing tickets, records or code) are identified, and which of those actions need human review and how that review is set up is defined.

The risks of each vendor's AI are assessed and documented before and during use: its model provider, data retention and training use, terms of service, the vendor's security and tenant isolation, and what happens when the AI feature fails or is unavailable.
The controls for each vendor AI feature (training opt-out, history retention off, risky features disabled, which data classes may go to it) are identified and documented.

The likelihood and magnitude of harm from each vendor's AI use of the org's data (by data classification, retention or training at the model provider) are assessed, so vendor AI features are ranked by impact.
Vendor AI features are watched in use for changes the vendor makes without notice, such as new features, defaults, models or data handling.
The security of vendor AI features is evaluated, including how they handle hostile content in the org's data (prompt injection) and the vendor's own security test evidence.
Vendor AI activity on the org's data (who invoked it, what it read and changed) is logged and the vendor's logs are collected so actions can be traced.
Staff using a vendor's AI feature can report problems with it (wrong actions, unexpected data use), and these reports feed the evaluation of that vendor feature.
Before a vendor AI feature is turned on or kept on, the org decides whether it meets its purpose and risk requirements, with features off by default until then.
The org can switch off a vendor AI feature, with someone responsible and set thresholds, when it misbehaves or the vendor changes how it uses the org's data.
Each vendor's AI is monitored regularly for changes (new features, model provider, terms) and the agreed controls are checked as still applied.
When a vendor or its AI feature is dropped, the org's data held by the vendor and its model provider is deleted and access revoked.
Incidents involving a vendor's AI and the org's data are reported to and from the vendor, tracked and responded to, with vendor contacts kept current.
The purpose and business value of building or tuning the model, its intended uses, users and the settings it will be released into are written down before the build starts.
The people who build and tune the model bring the range of skills, domain and user experience and backgrounds needed to spot bias and misuse in what it is built for, and who took part is documented.
Requirements such as security, privacy and safety are set for the model being built or tuned and shape choices from base model selection to release.
The task the built or tuned model performs and the method used (base model, tuning approach, model type) are defined and documented, for example in a model card, with their assumptions and limits.
rows.review_reason: LLM-16.4 (AI/Model BOM of provenance, integrity and dependencies) is evidence for the component inventory in MAP 4.1, not for defining the model's task and method; the safeguard moved here from the dropped MEASURE 2.9 row without fitting this outcome.

rows.why: Each released version comes with documentation telling recipients its knowledge limits, uses outside its intended scope and how its output should be overseen.
The base models, libraries and other third-party components used to build or tune the model are inventoried with their source, licence and intellectual property risks.
Controls are applied to base models and components before use, such as integrity checks and review for poisoning, backdoors and unsafe code.
Each built or tuned version is evaluated for safety before release, for example that tuning has not stripped safety behaviour, and shown to fail safely when used beyond its knowledge limits.
The built or tuned model is red-teamed and threat-modelled for security weaknesses such as backdoors inherited from a base model before release.
Building and tuning runs, base model and component choices, changes and releases are logged so that who did what to each version can be traced.
The energy use and environmental impact of training and tuning the model are estimated and documented.
Recipients of a released model have a way to report problems with it, and the reports feed back into building and tuning.
A go or no-go decision is made on whether a built or tuned version meets its purpose before it is released to others.
A problem found in a released model is responded to and recovered from by a defined procedure that covers rebuilding and restoring it
A released model version can be withdrawn or superseded, with set thresholds and responsibilities, when it behaves outside its intended use.
The pre-trained base models and the third-party libraries and frameworks the build relies on are monitored for new vulnerabilities and issues, and replaced when they exceed risk tolerance.
Changes to building or tuning integrate recipient feedback and are assessed against requirements and trade-offs before a new version replaces the previous one.
Incidents and errors in a released model are communicated to its recipients, and a version history records each change to building or tuning and why.
Why staff use unapproved AI, the benefit they get from it, is understood, and approved alternatives are checked to meet that need.

The org finds and lists the AI tools, features, PoCs and local models staff use without approval, what data they receive and where it goes, and the outside AI agents connecting in, not only the approved ones.
Controls that stop staff installing or reaching unvetted AI (software safelists, blocked AI services, restricted AI browser extensions) are identified and documented.
For the unapproved AI use and outside agents it finds, the org assesses how likely and how serious the harm is (what data, how sensitive, how often), to prioritise treatment.
Staff are regularly engaged to surface the AI tools and experiments they use and the needs behind them, so unseen use and its impacts come to light.
Endpoints, network traffic and logs are monitored continuously to detect new unapproved AI tools, local model runners and agent or MCP software as they appear.
AI tools, browser extensions, local model runtimes and MCP or agent packages staff installed from unvetted public sources are checked for malicious code and known vulnerabilities.
Use of unapproved AI services and locally installed AI software is logged and attributable to the person, so what was used and when can be traced and reviewed.
The risk of personal and sensitive data leaving through unapproved AI tools is examined, including checks on data sent to public AI services.
For each AI tool or experiment found in unapproved use, a decision is made whether it serves a real purpose and is brought under approval and support, or must stop.
Access staff can grant to AI tools (OAuth consents, tokens, delegated permissions running with their privileges) is controlled, centralised and reviewed for excess.
Unapproved AI software can be removed or blocked, and the access staff granted to AI tools is revoked when they leave or change role.
Incidents from unapproved AI use, such as data pasted into a public AI service, are reported, tracked, responded to and reviewed.
Requirements are set for each AI system on which data classes may be put into prompts, pasted text and files, and how inputs are minimised or sanitised before they reach the model.
For each external model provider receiving prompts and files, the terms on retention, reuse for training and data location are reviewed and the flow of inputs to that provider is documented.
The controls that stop sensitive data going into prompts and uploads (DLP, sanitisation, user guidance on what may be pasted) are identified and documented for each AI system and provider.
Prompts and uploads in production are monitored for sensitive data and unexpected patterns, with alerts when inputs break the set rules.

The input controls (DLP, sanitisation, blocking of unapproved AI services) are tested to show they stop sensitive data in prompts and uploads and cannot easily be bypassed, including pasted text and files carrying injected instructions.
Prompts and responses are logged as a record with who sent what, who can read those logs , so exposure can be traced and accounted for.

Personal and sensitive data in prompts and files, and what staff and systems send in production (volumes, file types, unexpected input), are monitored, with alerts when sensitive data appears or leaves the org.
Prompt and response logs are kept only as long as set, access to them is restricted, they are encrypted, and they are securely deleted, including on deletion requests.
Sending prompts and files to a provider or AI tool can be cut off quickly (blocking the endpoint, disabling uploads) when inputs are found to leak sensitive data, with set thresholds for doing so.
Exposures of sensitive input are recorded and communicated to the affected people, providers and regulators after they are found.

notes.reason: The row also tests how pasted text and files carrying injected instructions are handled, but the area's threat speaks only of sensitive data leaving the org; the threat may be too narrow.

rows.why: The intended purpose and settings of the AI's answers, and what counts as a correct answer for them, are defined, so accuracy, consistency and bias tests have a target.
Requirements for the AI's answers (the accuracy, consistency and fairness levels they must meet) are set with the people who rely on them and understood by those who build, test and run the AI.
The knowledge limits of the AI's answers (topics, conditions and questions where it is unreliable) and how its output is meant to be used and checked are documented for those who rely on it.
How the AI's answers are to be tested for accuracy, consistency and bias is designed and documented: test design, how test cases are chosen and whether they represent real questions.
The costs of wrong, made-up, inconsistent or biased answers, and who or what they could harm, are examined against the organisation's risk tolerance.
The likelihood and impact of wrong or attacker-steered answers (prompt injection, poisoned answers) are identified using threat modelling, red teaming and known public incidents.
Accuracy, consistency and bias tests of answers are done or reviewed by people other than those who built the system (independent assessors, domain experts, affected users).
The test sets, metrics and tools used to test answers for accuracy, consistency and bias are documented, with how the test data was chosen and why the tests measure what they claim.
Answer quality is measured before deployment under conditions like real use, including realistic and non-optimised questions, and the results are documented.
Answer quality is monitored in production against pre-deployment results, with alerts when accuracy drifts or anomalous answers appear.
The AI's answers are shown to be accurate and consistent (the same question gives the same answer) before deployment, and the limits beyond which this was not shown are documented.
The AI is tested for how it behaves beyond its knowledge limits, so it declines or flags uncertainty instead of making up facts, and downstream fail-safes hold against bad answers.
The AI's answers are tested adversarially for prompt injection through user input or retrieved content, jailbreaks and unsafe or steered output, and results are documented.
The AI's answers are logged with the request that produced them and who received them, so a wrong or steered answer can be traced and reviewed.
Answers are presented with enough context (basis, confidence, limits) for people to judge how far to trust them before acting.
The AI's answers are evaluated for bias, whether they treat people or groups unequally, with results documented per group.
The metrics and tests used to judge answer quality are reviewed for whether they actually catch wrong, inconsistent and biased answers.
Domain experts and users confirm that answers are valid, reliable and consistent in real use.
Baselines for answer quality are kept and changes after model, prompt or data updates are measured, so declines in accuracy or consistency are found.
Test results on answer accuracy, consistency and bias are used to decide whether the AI is good enough to deploy or keep in use.
Controls such as guardrails, output filtering and business rules limit or restrict what answers the AI can give in a given context.
When a new way the AI's answers go wrong or are steered is found (a new injection or failure mode), there is a procedure to respond and recover.
Thresholds and mechanisms exist to stop relying on, bypass or switch off the AI when its answers fall below the intended quality.
Findings and feedback on wrong, inconsistent or biased answers are fed into model, prompt or data updates as measurable improvements to answer quality.
Wrong, harmful or biased answers are recorded as errors or incidents, tracked to resolution and communicated to those affected.
How training, tuning and evaluation data are collected and selected (availability, representativeness, suitability) and how the test harness is designed is identified and documented.
The sources of training, tuning and test data, including third-party and public datasets and reused feedback, are inventoried with the licence or other right to use each for training.

Controls protecting datasets and the evaluation harness from poisoning and tampering (access, separation of who curates data from who trains, isolation, encryption) are identified and documented, including for third-party data.
Evaluation sets and the harness are held or reviewed by people independent of the developers, so they cannot be changed to hide failures.
The test sets, metrics and harness tools used to evaluate the model are documented and versioned, so a result can be traced to the exact data and test cases used.
Datasets built from people's data are collected with consent and human-subject protections and are checked to be representative of the population the model will serve.
The evaluation and test sets are checked to reflect the conditions the model will be deployed in, including non-optimised and edge cases, not only clean or convenient data.
The harness and evaluation sets are checked to be valid, so the test cases measure what they claim and results are not inflated by overlap with the training data.
Training, tuning and evaluation data are tested for poisoning, injected records and tampering before use, and the results are documented.
Changes to training, tuning and evaluation datasets and to the harness are logged with who made them and when, so tampering can be traced and accounted for.
Personal and sensitive data in training sets and in feedback or logs reused for tuning is found, minimised or removed, and access to it is controlled.
The evaluation sets and harness are reviewed to confirm they still catch known failures and have not been weakened or become stale.

When poisoned, tampered or unlawfully used data is discovered, the models trained or evaluated on it are identified, the data is restored from a clean copy, and the incident is recorded, reported to the owners of the affected models and reviewed.
rows.review_reason: also_covers still names MANAGE 4.3, but the why reports the incident only to the owners of the affected models; it does not tell the users of those models or the people whose data was unlawfully used (affected communities), which the round-1 finding asked for.

rows.why: Third-party and public datasets and benchmarks are monitored for licence changes, withdrawals and reported contamination, and the risk controls applied are documented.
Deletion and rectification requests are tracked through to the training, tuning and evaluation datasets and reused feedback that hold the affected data.
User feedback and logs are vetted for quality, sensitive data and manipulation before they are reused to tune or update the model.

missing.reason: Dropped from MANAGE 2.3's also_covers and now unmapped: nothing checks that a poisoned or unlawfully used dataset can be pulled from training and evaluation pipelines and that models trained or evaluated on it are stopped or replaced.

rows.why: Protection requirements for the model are set at design: which weights, versions, system prompts and configurations must stay confidential or unaltered, and what may be exposed through its API.
The legal and IP risks of the model as an asset are mapped: who owns the weights and versions, the licence they are released under, and the risk of the model leaking or infringing rights.
The likelihood and impact of the model being stolen, copied, extracted through its API or tampered with are assessed and documented.
Use of the model in production is monitored for extraction patterns and for signs that the deployed version or its configuration differs from the approved one.
The model's resistance to extraction through its API, weight theft and version tampering is tested, for example by red-teaming, and the results are documented.
Access to weights, prompts and configurations, and changes to model versions, are logged so copying or tampering can be traced to who did it.
Controls such as restricted access, encryption and protected backups are applied to weights, fine-tuned versions and system prompts.
When a version is found tampered with or leaked, it is taken out of use and a known-good version of the weights, prompts and configuration is restored from protected backups.
The third-party base weights under the fine-tuned versions are verified and monitored for tampering, licence or support changes, and withdrawn when they exceed risk tolerance.
Changes to model versions, system prompts and parameters go through change management with version control and pinning, so unapproved changes are caught after deployment.
Incidents of model theft, extraction, leaked system prompts or tampered versions are reported, tracked, communicated to those affected and reviewed afterwards.
Requirements for the store (who may see which content through the AI, privacy and entitlement expectations) are set, and retrieval entitlements follow them.
What the store does not cover, and where answers built on it should not be relied on, is documented and told to users so they know when to check elsewhere.
The content chosen for the store is checked for provenance, suitability and currency before it is indexed, so the AI does not answer from unsuitable or untrusted sources.
The benefit of connecting each store to the AI is documented, so the exposure it opens can be weighed against what it is meant to deliver.

The likelihood and the harm of the store leaking data to the wrong asker, being copied out through the AI or being poisoned are examined against the organisation's risk tolerance and the data's classification.
Which data and which classification levels each store may hold is set according to who can query the AI that retrieves from it.
The retrieval stores and the data sources feeding them, including third-party and licensed content, are inventoried with their owners and any rights or licence limits on use by the AI.

The controls on the store are identified and documented: classification, access rights carried into retrieval, protection against unauthorised change, encryption and segmentation from untrusted inputs.
Changes to the store's content and retrieval patterns are monitored in use to spot poisoning, unexpected content and attempts to pull sensitive data through the AI.
Retrieval fails safely: it refuses rather than exposing restricted content when permission or classification checks fail or the store misbehaves.
The store is tested for whether an asker can retrieve content beyond their own rights, whether injected content changes answers and whether bulk content can be extracted through the AI.
Retrievals are logged with who asked and which documents were returned, and changes to the store are recorded, so exposure of data through the AI can be traced.
Personal data held in the store is identified and the privacy risk of it being disclosed or inferred through AI answers is examined.
Users and data owners can report that the AI exposed content they should not see or answered from wrong content, and these reports feed the store's evaluation.
The store is kept current and clean: outdated content is removed, deletion and correction requests reach the index and embeddings, and retention is applied.
When store content is found poisoned or leaked, it is cleaned, re-indexed and access reviewed by a defined procedure that is followed in practice.
A store or a part of its content can be disconnected from the AI quickly when it leaks or gives poisoned answers, with someone assigned to decide this.
Third-party and external content feeding the store is monitored over time, and its risks controlled, not only identified when it is added.
Data exposed or altered through the store is reported to the data owners and affected people, and such incidents and changes to the store are tracked.

notes.reason: Failing safely when a question is outside the store's coverage or the store is unavailable addresses wrong answers, which the area's threat (exposure, poisoning, copy-out) does not mention; the threat may be too narrow.

rows.why: The connections each AI tool or MCP server opens to internal systems, outside providers and the internet are documented, with which tool actions people oversee.

The harm a tool call could do if the AI misuses its permissions, or is steered by an attacker, is assessed for how likely and how severe it is, against the assets and data the tool reaches and the users whose machines run it.
The tools and capabilities enabled for each AI use are limited to what that use needs, and new tools or capabilities on a known server are not used until reviewed.
Tool actions that need a person to confirm them before they run (writes, deletes, payments, external sends) are identified, and the confirmation is enforced.
The MCP servers and tools the AI can call, hosted inside or used from outside, are inventoried with who runs them, what each can reach, the asset it runs on and the credentials it uses.
Internal controls for each tool or MCP server (approval before use, allowed versions) are identified and documented.
The approved tools and MCP servers in production are monitored for unusual use and for changes to the tools or capabilities they offer, and deviations from what was approved are caught.
The AI fails safely when a tool or MCP server errors, times out, is unavailable or returns something unexpected, instead of retrying or leaving partial changes.
Tools and MCP servers are tested against attacks such as tool poisoning, prompt injection through tool output and abuse of their permissions, and the results are recorded.
Tool calls are logged with the user, client and credentials behind them, including on outside servers, so every action the AI takes can be traced and accounted for.
The personal data each tool can read or send out with its credentials is examined, and tool egress is watched so personal data is not exposed or exfiltrated through tool calls.
Access to tools is granted through a set process with credentials scoped to least privilege for the AI, not sized for a human or borrowed from the user, and reviewed against actual use.
A tool or MCP server can be disabled or removed and its tokens and sessions revoked quickly, with someone responsible for doing so.
Outside MCP servers and their providers are monitored for version, capability and authorization changes and advisories, and kept to supported, trusted versions.
Post-deployment monitoring of tools covers change management for new tools or permissions and decommissioning of unused tools.
Incidents involving tools, such as unauthorized tool calls, a compromised server or stolen tokens, are reported, contained, reviewed and shared with the server's operators.
Each agent's intended task, the processes it acts in, its business owner and the degree of autonomy it is meant to have are documented.
Each agent's limits, the situations and settings outside its approved use, and its dependencies on the other agents and systems it calls or is called by along a chain are documented.
The benefit that justifies giving the agent autonomy (time saved, error rate against a person doing the task) is examined with its users.

The likelihood and cost of agent errors, including chained actions, irreversible changes and actions triggered by manipulated input or poisoned memory, are examined and documented against the organisation's risk tolerance.
Each agent's scope of action is narrowed and documented: which systems, tools, data and kinds of action it may touch, and which it may not.
The agent actions that need human approval or review (for example irreversible or high-impact changes) are identified and the oversight process for them is defined.
The third-party components an agent is built from (orchestration frameworks, models, memory stores, plug-ins) are inventoried and their technology and legal risks mapped.
The components an agent is built on (models, orchestration frameworks, libraries, executors) are inventoried and held to approved versions, with their legal, IP and supply-chain risks documented.
The likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions are assessed, including irreversible changes and actions triggered by manipulated input.
The agent's task performance is measured in conditions like the real deployment (real systems, messy inputs), not only in tests.
Agent behaviour in production is monitored for anomalies such as unexpected tool calls, runaway loops, cost spikes or unusual decision paths, with alerts on thresholds.
The agent is shown to complete its tasks within its autonomy limits under realistic conditions, and where it must not act on its own is documented.
Agents are shown to fail safely when they meet situations beyond their limits, stopping or escalating instead of continuing a chain of actions, with circuit breakers tested.
Agents are red-teamed against manipulated input, memory poisoning, hijacking of their access and sandbox breakout, and the results are documented.
Every agent action, tool call, memory access and hand-off to another agent is logged against a unique agent identity and the person it acts for, so actions can be traced end to end.
Privacy risk from personal data the agent keeps in memory across sessions and moves between systems by its actions is examined.
Staff and operators working alongside agents can report unexpected agent actions, and these reports feed the evaluation of the agents.
A decision is made and recorded, based on testing, whether an agent may go into production and at what level of autonomy.
Controls keep agents within their scope in use: least-privilege identities, separate credentials per component, allowlisted tools and scripts, and business rules limiting what actions they can take.
Agents can be stopped or disconnected quickly when they act outside intended use, with thresholds that trigger it, named people responsible and a fallback for the process.
Third-party agent platforms and outside agents in an agent chain are monitored, with trusted, supported components and provider logs collected.
Post-deployment plans for each agent cover change management of its configuration and tools, and retiring agents that are no longer needed.
Agent incidents are handled by people who understand agent failure modes, communicated to affected parties and providers, and reviewed through the chain of actions, memory and tool outputs.

missing.reason: With also_covers dropped from MAP 3.3, nothing checks that the requirements for an agent (what it shall and shall not do alone, when it must hand back to a person) are elicited from the operators and the people it acts for, and that design decisions weigh the socio-technical effect of removing human oversight.

rows.why: The hosting's deployment settings are documented: who calls the serving endpoints (the org's own products or a consumer's PoC), where the hosting runs, and which laws apply there, such as data residency.
The business case for hosting the model on the org's own infrastructure rather than using a provider's API, including GPU spend, is defined and re-evaluated.
Requirements for hosting the model (availability, capacity, isolation, spending limits, key handling) are set before serving endpoints are built.
The hosting's connections are documented: which networks and the internet can reach the serving endpoints, and which systems depend on them.

The cost of a hosting compromise, an outage of the serving endpoints and runaway or abused GPU spend is examined against the risk tolerance, with the likelihood and magnitude of each rated on a set scale.
The hosting components (servers, GPUs, model registry, serving runtimes, secrets stores) and the third-party hardware, cloud and software they rely on are inventoried.
The controls on each hosting component are identified: hardened configuration, host firewalls, network isolation, allowlisted runtimes and scoped secrets.

Hosting is monitored in production against set baselines for availability, load, GPU spend and anomalous traffic or host changes, and changes after runtime or driver updates are checked and recorded as improvements or declines.
Serving infrastructure is stress-tested under high load and failure, and shown to fail safely rather than expose the model or run up cost.
The security and resilience of the hosting are evaluated: vulnerability scans of hosts and exposed endpoints, penetration tests and recovery tests.
Access to hosts, the model registry, serving endpoints and keys is logged with identity, so compromise and cost abuse can be traced.
The energy use and efficiency of the GPUs and servers hosting the model are measured against set baselines.
Controls that protect the hosted service are applied: authenticated access, network isolation, throttling, firewalling, scoped secrets and keys, and a hardened serving configuration.

Incidents on the hosting (compromise, outage, leaked keys, cost abuse) are responded to and recovered from under a rehearsed procedure, recorded and tracked, and communicated to those affected, such as consumers whose PoC runs on the hosting.
Serving endpoints can be taken offline and keys revoked when thresholds are crossed, with backups or failover to restore service.
Third-party cloud, GPU and serving-software providers the hosting relies on are monitored, with their risks and support tracked.
Post-deployment plans for the hosting environment cover patching and change management of the hosting stack.
